ubs.subject: UBS: Oracle Corporation "Creditors Applaud, Hence So Do We" (Buy) Keirstead
ubs.reviewed_text:
The ability to self-fund capex growth beyond FY27 comes as a major relief to
credit as well as equity holders.  
|  |  | Global Research   
28 October 2026  
---|---|---  
| Oracle Corporation| ●| (ORCL.N) Buy|  
---|---|---|---  
| Creditors Applaud, Hence So Do
We  
---  
| The ability to self-fund capex growth beyond FY27 comes as a major relief to
credit as well as equity holders.  
  
| | Read Report   > |   
---|---  
| Summary The focus of equity investors into the Oracle Investor Day in Vegas
was not about revs, demand and GPU pricing (all positive, but all well-
understood). Rather, it was on the subjects that credit investors typically
care more about – the path to being FCF positive and how much debt financing
Oracle will need. As such, if credit investors came away positive, so would
we. Oracle delivered what both credit and equity investors had hoped for and
more – FCF positive earlier than expected, no debt/equity funding needed
beyond FY27 and a reaffirm of the MT guide. We remain BUY-rated. Best-Case
Credit Story Oracle disclosed: 1. It would reach FCF positive in 2H FY28
(Feb/May 2028 quarters), two quarters earlier than we modeled. 2. After
raising another $20b of debt/equity through the remainder of FY27 (expected),
Oracle will fully-fund its capex thereafter (no need for external debt/equity
funding). This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt
markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt
market concerns have been over-stated). 3. This is not happening because
Oracle is throttling growth and therefore capex (in fact our FY28 capex
estimate is moving UP). Rather, it’s because Oracle is making a harder pivot
to alternative funding sources, including a) vendor financing (we assume a
large portion from Nvidia, which Oracle said is “largely solidified” but “one
can’t be presumptuous”), b) bring-your-own-chip deals (customers acquire the
chips, Oracle deploys/manages) and c) more customer pre-payments. Bottom line,
these measures protect Oracle’s IG rating and reduce the credit risk and we’re
raising our FY29 FCF estimate materially. Other Observations/Readthroughs We
conclude: 1. This is a positive read to CoreWeave, as it strengthens the
conviction that they too can access these non-debt funding alternatives (which
we described in a note last week, see
here). 2. The reaffirm of the MT EPS guide, which the Street was
discounting, is impressive as Oracle is absorbing the earnings impact (lower
prices given pre-pays, vendor financing costs) of asking suppliers/customers
to fund its capex. 3. We noted less focus on the core database business,
implying to us that Oracle is not seeing the previously-stated revs accretion
from the cloud database migrations. 4. Oracle did not flag any systemic delays
in adding GW of data center capacity (to reach 10GW by year-end FY28).
Valuation: At ~16x CY27E non-GAAP EPS and at ~11x our revised FY30 FCF
estimate, we remain Buy-rated on a view that the revs growth acceleration and
margin durability is better than feared. Our unchanged PT of $250 is based on
a CY28E non-GAAP multiple of 19x, a justified premium relative to peers, in
our view.  
---  
| 
| Karl Keirstead,
Analyst

ms_credit.subject: PULSE: TMT Credit Research: ORCL Credit: More Cards on the Table
ms_credit.reviewed_text:
| | | |   
---  
  
---  
| | |   
---  
TMT Credit Research  
ORCL Credit: More Cards on the Table  
| | Read Full Report  
---  
(PDF: 10 Pages)  
---  
| North America  
---  
Lindsay A Tyler, Benjamin Guerrero  
October 29, 2026  
---  
In attending Oracle’s AI World and Analyst Day in Las Vegas, we saw firsthand
management’s commitment to an ambitious AI infrastructure buildout and
appreciated the breadth of new detail, though questions remain. With ORCL
paper having widened materially over the past couple of months, we tactically
anticipated a rally-then-reverse response in our preview note, which largely
played out, albeit with a more bullish overall reaction than expected. New CFO
Maxson’s comprehensive funding commentary was a pleasant surprise relative to
prior years. ORCL bond and CDS spreads tightened as much as ~40bp before
retracing roughly half the move. Sellers emerged at tighter levels, with 10Y
and 30Y cash spreads and 5Y CDS then still settling around 245/285/275bp,
respectively, underscoring the risks that remain embedded in the credit
(Exhibit 1, Exhibit 2).A clearer financing roadmap, though with tradeoffs:
Management reiterated its IG commitment and ~$20bn FY27 remaining funding
need, as expected, but went further with several new targets:

  * Capital markets funding: Management outlined that the FY27 $20bn remaining FY27 will now be split evenly between debt and equity, with no further external capital expected thereafter (excl. refinancing). We’ve long flagged the need to manage ORCL’s growing US IG index footprint, and management now appears to be taking an even more conservative approach to debt issuance than our illustrative funding path. We flagged more recently one potential funding implication of higher rates may be pulling issuance in on the curve. The implied and now-awaited ~$10bn bond deal will probably be weighted toward the belly rather than the long end, supporting curve flattening.
  * Leverage: Management is now targeting net leverage (incl. leases) <3.5x by FY29 (Exhibit 3), though our prior FY29E net adjusted leverage forecast was already ~3.25x. That is still an elevated metric for what we typically see in IG TMT. (The 3.5x figure recalls a threshold in the Cerner-era bond prospectus, albeit on a gross rather than adjusted net basis and tied to resuming buybacks.)
  * FCF and revenue: Management guided to positive FCF in F2H28, self-funded growth beginning in FY29 and $30bn+ of FY29 FCF, the latter particularly constructive vs. just under $20bn estimate. It also added a “+” to its prior $225bn FY30 revenue target.
  * Vendor financing and leases: Beyond future FCF growth, what else reduces funding needs? Management outlined ~5-year vendor financing (Exhibit 6), reminding us of Larry Ellison's September 2025 comments on ORCL's ability to secure favorable equipment financing. We expect principal repayments to fall under financing cash flows, outside reported FCF, though this remains unconfirmed. We also wonder whether arrangements could include 5-year GPU or TPU leases, in turn backing debt, aligning payments with customer revenue, despite management's dismissal of structured financing using "Oracle credit out in the market" during Q&A. While easing traditional funding needs, such arrangements remain debt-like and potentially less transparent. Notably, management provided no ceiling on future lease liabilities.
  * Capex through FY28: Management framed ~$220bn of illustrative capex need related to 6GW from FY2Q27 through FY28 (Exhibit 5), above our prior ~$180bn estimate in partnership with our equity colleagues.
  * Buildout economics, progress and scale: Updated illustrative economics suggested ~$37bn of capex over two years supporting ~$16bn of annualized revenue at full ramp, implying greater upfront investment but improved revenue-per-watt economics for new signings. On potential delays at large sites, ORCL offered little site-specific progress beyond Abilene. Instead, management emphasized that large sites account for only ~5GW of the broader buildout, consistent with prior disclosures, and explained the rationale for a mix of large and smaller sites with varying power solutions. We also continue to sense longer-term ambitions may extend beyond the disclosed >10GW build (Exhibit 4).
  * Compute fungibility and contracts: We appreciated OCI leadership’s color on compute fungibility, time from power availability to revenue, and implied MW delivery per day from FY1Q27, but learned little about actual contract terms, including termination rights and protections for both sides.

We maintain our medium-term cautious stance and 5Y CDS and 10Y cash
recommendations, though our caution has moderated of late given improved
spread compensation following such sizable CY2H widening, greater visibility
from the Analyst Day and more constructive credit and equity sentiment. Three
lingering concerns: (1) favorable funding technicals should not overshadow
fundamental risks around leverage (increasingly in less transparent debt-like
forms), contract/lease mismatches, execution and counterparty concentration;
(2) ORCL spreads remain highly sensitive to the broader macro and AI ecosystem
backdrop; and (3) CDS and front-end/belly cash face an IG AI supply overhang,
potentially compounded by bespoke, off-index chip financing offering higher
ratings and wider spreads. We see a path for ORCL 10Y paper to return to the
275bp area on a bond deal, vendor financing disclosure, or site-specific
headline.We close our sell recommendation on ORCL 5.95% 55s (opened 1/23/26 at
+208bp). We recognize that fundamental risks and macro sensitivity could still
push long-bond spreads back toward +300bp. However, we increasingly prefer
expressing our maintained cautious view in the front-end/belly, given likely
limited long-end issuance versus potentially sizable shorter-dated, debt-like
financing at ORCL and across the AI ecosystem. Our decision to close reflects
this relative preference rather than a dismissal of long-end risks. We've
taken into account lower-quality comms/media comps and curves._See our preview
from Monday:ORCL Credit: What Happens in Vegas Won't Stay in Vegas (26 Oct
2026),
as well as select key Analyst Day slides and other exhibits next in the
Appendix below._ Read
more...|  
---

jpm.subject: JPM ANMUTH - Alphabet: Navigable Cross Currents or Structural Search Slowdown?
jpm.reviewed_text:
| |  | North America Equity Research  
---|---  
  
# Alphabet

## Navigable Cross Currents or Structural Search Slowdown?

  
---  
  
By Doug Anmuth
AC,
Dae K Lee,
CFA,
Margaret
Hoffman

Click here for the full document and
disclaimers

| Overweight  
---  
GOOG, GOOG US  
Price (28 Oct 26):$321.89  
**▼** Price Target (Dec-27):$375.00  
Prior (Dec-27):$425.00  
Overweight  
---  
GOOGL, GOOGL US  
Price (28 Oct 26):$324.89  
**▼** Price Target (Dec-27):$375.00  
Prior (Dec-27):$425.00  
|   
---  
  
Alphabet’s 3Q results & the stock’s sharp move lower show us the margin for
error when a hyperscaler spending hundreds of billions on the AI
infrastructure buildout and flipping to negative FCF posts disappointing
results in the core. Not that there was much debate going in—most investors
seemed to understand that strong Google Cloud growth, including early TPU
ramp, wouldn’t be enough to offset a Search shortfall, which was telegraphed
in 3P data. But the magnitude of Search deceleration—from +16.8% in 2Q to
+12.0% in 3Q—was steeper than expected, w/discussions in the +13-14% range.
Google faced a tough search comp in 3Q, and management indicated that FX was
the single largest driver of the decel. We estimate FX impact in Search
flipped from ~100bps tailwind in 2Q to ~80bps headwind in 3Q. The company also
called out slower APAC retailer spend related to the EU eliminating the de
minimis exemption, along w/normalized media & entertainment vertical
advertising post the 2Q World Cup bump. But with Google delivering its
strongest query growth in 5 years, it’s AI Mode monetization headwinds that
will get the most scrutiny. AI Mode is becoming a bigger % of search queries &
we believe it lags traditional search in both coverage & ad load, resulting in
lower overall monetization. Google announced the expansion of ads in AI Mode
to international markets, which should help, but the monetization gap will
likely bring back concerns from a couple years ago about a potential AI Search
air pocket. Search shortfall (high margin revenue) likely contributed to lower
Google Services margin—40.7% vs. our 43.5% estimate—and we also believe legal
charges in G&A pressured Services margins. While some of that can be explained
away, further margin pressure on Alphabet overall, and Google Cloud
specifically, begins in 4Q w/the bridge compute deal w/SPCX for $920M/month or
an estimated ~$50/GW. More positively, Google Cloud grew 103% & Google’s new
Gemini Carbon model ranks at the top of the updated Artificial Analysis
Intelligence Index, ranking above the frontier labs. Importantly, Carbon,
Google’s strongest model to date, shows an accelerated launch cadence,
w/release less than a month after Gemini 4 Argon. Google Cloud’s growth was
driven by both AI and core GCP, and we believe it still grew ~80% even without
an estimated ~$3B in TPU sales. Overall, there’s a lot to like about Google on
the Cloud, AI, and models side of the business, and we now project Google
Cloud revenue surpasses Search—and AMZN’s AWS—in the first half of 2028. But
Search also faces tough comps & bigger FX headwinds in 4Q, & AI Mode
monetization may take some time to kick in. This could keep pressure on Google
shares near-term, or make them range-bound. The positive catalysts would
likely be further model releases and agentic product build-out, which we’re
optimistic could be impactful as a consumer-focused personal agent is
integrated into Gemini, which has 1B+ users. We’re sticking Overweight, as we
believe Google’s Search headwinds are more navigable than permanently
structural, and Google Cloud becomes an even more critical part of the
business, driving overall Alphabet revenue growth of ~30% in both 2027 & 2028.
Still, our GAAP EPS estimates for 2027 and 2028 come down -5% and -2%, and
we’re lowering our price target from $425 to $375 based on 22x 2028E GAAP EPS
of $17.00.

  * Search Engagement Strong, But Revenue Growth Pressured. Search & other revenue growth of +12% Y/Y came in below expectations despite Y/Y query growth accelerating to its highest rate in the past five years. The deceleration from +16.8% in 2Q mainly reflects: 1) A ~3 point tougher comp reported, & ~2 pts tougher FXN; 2) FX headwinds, w/almost a 2 point swing from 2Q; 3) APAC retailers impacted by the EU eliminating its de minimis exemption; & 4) Normalization of Media & Entertainment spend after World Cup-driven strength in 2Q. Additionally, while Google believes the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, monetization remains lower vs. traditional Search, which likely adds to the disconnect between engagement & revenue growth. However, Google is focused on scaling ads across both AI Overviews & AI Mode to more users, queries, & geos, and believes click through rates are similar between sponsored and organic product items within AI Mode. That said, we expect Search growth to remain pressured N-T, with Y/Y comps continuing to get tougher through 1Q27, 4Q FX headwinds expected to be slightly larger relative to 3Q, & limited visibility into recovery of APAC retailers impacted by the de minimis change. We now model Search & other revenue growth of +9% Y/Y (+10% FXN) in 4Q & 2027\. 
  * Broad-Based Cloud Growth w/TPUs Beginning to Scale. Cloud revenue grew +103% Y/Y driven by GCP, just above our +100% estimate, with strength in both AI & core GCP. Momentum remains strong across a wide range of products, customers, & industries, with 18 product lines generating over $1B each in annual revenue. Google’s 1P model APIs are now processing ~32B tokens per minute, over 2,600 customers have used 100B+ tokens over the past 12 months, & Gemini Enterprise adoption remains strong with 100M+ seats sold for knowledge work. TPU system sales were also a meaningful contributor to 3Q Cloud revenue & the company is seeing strong demand across a wide range of customers, including recent deals with Oracle & Crux AI. Google clarified that when it signs an agreement to sell its TPU systems (which includes hardware, software, optical networking, etc.), the impact will first show up in backlog, and then Google will start to build inventory to serve that customer before it begins delivering the TPUs & recognizing revenue. Google continues to expect TPU contribution to scale through 4Q, followed by a more meaningful ramp in 2027, & is very focused on continuing to improve margins as the business scales. Additionally, the cloud backlog increased +$47B Q/Q to $561B, which remains majority typical GCP contracts & just over 55% of the backlog is expected to convert to revenue in the next 24 months. We project Cloud revenue growth of +111% in 4Q & +107% in 2027, including $5B & $57B of TPU revenue, respectively. 
  * AI Investments Continue to Ramp. 3Q Cloud operating margin of 36.2% exceeded expectations, but was offset by lighter than expected Services margin, likely reflecting slower Search growth & legal charges. Google began utilizing 3P bridging capacity (w/SPCX) at the very end of 3Q, limiting margin pressure in the quarter, though usage is set to ramp in 4Q & should result in a more meaningful N-T headwind to margins. Additionally, higher depreciation & data center operating costs should further weigh on the P&L as technical infrastructure investment scales. Mgmt maintained the 2026 capex guide of $195B-$205B & continues to expect a significant increase in 2027, which, together with the inventory ramp needed to scale the TPU business, will further pressure FCF. We model 2027 capex of $379B (+86% Y/Y) & Operating Margin of 32.0%.

| Summary Despite high expectations into the print (Microsoft shares were a
consensus long), the company delivered a solid beat, marked by an Azure beat
(1Q/2Q actual/guide of 48%/50% relative to expects of 47%/47%), a reaffirm (no
raise) of the CY26 capex guide excluding the impact of a 3P capacity delay and
total revs/EPS actuals and guide that landed above our estimates. Microsoft
shares were a defensive play into the print and are even more so post the
print (given misses elsewhere). We are Buy-rated. Azure and M365/Copilot
Narratives Improve The Azure upside had a few sources, but one key one to call
out was the strength of OpenAI in the quarter, which correlates to higher
Azure growth via strong Astra AI model sales that get distributed via Azure.
Given that OpenAI is now 30%+ of Azure revs (higher accounting for indirect
sales), Azure growth could be more variable depending on large lab customer
growth. We’re raising our FY27 Azure growth estimates and are now modeling an
exit 4Q growth rate of 47%, up from our previous estimate of 43%. The Azure
print was a solid read to cloud infra peers but note that if a key driver was
OpenAI health, that is more idio to Microsoft near-term. We believe that the
M365 upside (a 1-point beat) was rooted in the price increases and solid
premium SKU sales, with Microsoft moving away from Copilot seat disclosures
(not provided) to revs/usage color. Capex, Margins and External Financing We’d
note: 1. Capex estimates for CY26 were trimmed slightly ($175b to $170b) but
entirely for a 3P capacity delay into 1H CY27 (second straight quarter of no
raise). For the Mar/Jun quarters, Microsoft signaled higher capex (a relief
for semis investors). 2. Microsoft did not change its guide for OMs to be down
100bps in FY27, and margin/EPS control remains very high. 3. Sensitive to
Meta’s recent equity raise, investors reacted negatively to Microsoft’s
comment about being open to external funding sources but post our call-back,
we believe that the likelihood of an equity raise is very low. Valuation: At
CY27E multiples of 24x GAAP EPS and 22x non-GAAP EPS, we still view the stock
as being reasonably priced, given growth accelerations in both Azure and M365,
strong EPS control and little need for external funding. We’re raising our PT
to $700 from $675, based on an assumed CY28 non-GAAP EPS multiple of 23x
(prior 25x) our raised CY28 estimates, a deserved premium to the peer group.

3Q Preview: Expect AWS to drive upside to estimates

Reports 10/29; we est. rev/EBIT at $202.0bn/$26.4bn vs Street at
$202.2bn/$26.1bn. We est. AWS growth of 40% y/y above Street at 38%, and we
expect upside to our ests. (+$4bn q/q rev. growth) driven by new capacity, YTD
price increases, ramp of AI Lab contracts, and growing enterprise inference
demand. We expect stable AWS margins at 39% in 3Q as higher depr. is offset by
strong utilization, growing Trainium workloads, Bedrock growth, and fee
increases. The key risk is high expectations (possibly at 42%+), but results
should suggest strong ROI on capacity capex.

Resilient Online retail spend in 3Q, Agentic in focus

Muse traction will likely drive questions on Amazon's agentic strategy. We
expect meet/beat sales as BAC aggregated credit & debit card data indicated
Online spend decelerated 4ppts q/q to 9% y/y, which is 6ppts better than
Street ests. for N.A. Retail growth to decelerate 10ppts q/q to 6% y/y. Ad
growth should decelerate due to Prime Day timing (we est 15% y/y growth vs 26%
in 2Q) but expect reacceleration in 4Q.

4Q Outlook: Expect 4Q guidance to bracket Street

Adobe ests. Oct. Big Deal Days sales was up 8.5%, while Amazon is upping
holiday hiring by 20%. For 4Q, slowing QTD Online retail spend is a risk, but
we expect rev. guidance of $239bn-$246bn (midpoint $242.5bn, +20% q/q), vs.
Street at $244.6bn. We expect an op. profit range of $29.0bn-$34.0bn vs.
Street at $32.9bn. AWS acceleration could drive 4Q profit upside, but 4Q is
driven by N.A. retail, where higher gas prices could be a 4Q margin headwind.

AWS positioning improving; Maintain Buy

Further improvement should be apparent in 3Q results that show AWS
acceleration and growing Bedrock & Trainium adoption aiding margins. Re:Invent
is a catalyst ahead that may have updates on Trainium 4, Bedrock, and possible
LLM development. Risks are capex growth & higher capital needs, 4Q cost
pressures from higher gas prices, and soft 3Q ad revs. (on Prime Day comp)
that fuel agentic concerns. Amazon's forward 2027E P/E multiple has contracted
from 29x (2025 YE) to 23x despite strong YTD results, so addressing Cloud
capacity ROI and Agentic risks to retail ad revenues could be key for stock
performance post print.
